questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Limit of a Rational Function with a Radical in the Numerator
questions.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{\sqrt{x+4}-2}{x} & =\frac{\sqrt{0+4}-2}{0}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the numerator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the numerator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{\sqrt{x+4}-2}{x} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{(\sqrt{x+4}-2)(\sqrt{x+4}+2)}{x(\sqrt{x+4}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x+4-4}{x(\sqrt{x+4}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+4}+2} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{0+4}+2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Limit of a Rational Function with a Radical in the Numerator
questions.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 4}\frac{\sqrt{2x-7}-1}{x-4} & =\frac{\sqrt{2(4)-7}-1}{4-4}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the numerator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the numerator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 4}\frac{\sqrt{2x-7}-1}{x-4} & ={lim}_{x\to 4}\frac{(\sqrt{2x-7}-1)(\sqrt{2x-7}+1)}{(x-4)(\sqrt{2x-7}+1)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 4}\frac{{(\sqrt{2x-7})}^{2}-{1}^{2}}{(x-4)(\sqrt{2x-7}+1)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 4}\frac{2x-7-1}{(x-4)(\sqrt{2x-7}+1)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 4}\frac{2x-8}{(x-4)(\sqrt{2x-7}+1)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 4}\frac{2(x-4)}{(x-4)(\sqrt{2x-7}+1)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 4}\frac{2}{\sqrt{2x-7}+1} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{2(4)-7}+1} \\  & =\frac{2}{1+1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Limit of a Rational Function with a Radical in the Numerator
questions.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 5}\frac{5-\sqrt{5x}}{5-x} & =\frac{5-\sqrt{5(5)}}{5-5}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the numerator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the numerator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 5}\frac{5-\sqrt{5x}}{5-x} & ={lim}_{x\to 5}\frac{(5-\sqrt{5x})(5+\sqrt{5x})}{(5-x)(5+\sqrt{5x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 5}\frac{{5}^{2}-{(\sqrt{5x})}^{2}}{(5-x)(5+\sqrt{5x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 5}\frac{25-5x}{(5-x)(5+\sqrt{5x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 5}\frac{5(5-x)}{(5-x)(5+\sqrt{5x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 5}\frac{5\cancel{(5-x)}}{\cancel{(5-x)}(5+\sqrt{5x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 5}\frac{5}{5+\sqrt{5x}} \\  & =\frac{5}{5+\sqrt{5(5)}} \\  & =\frac{5}{5+\sqrt{25}} \\  & =\frac{5}{10} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Limit of a Rational Function with a Radical in the Denominator
questions.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit by simply evaluating the function at $x=\frac{1}{4}$ we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1/4)}\frac{4x-1}{2x-\sqrt{x}} & =\frac{(4\cdot \frac{1}{4}-1)}{(2\cdot \frac{1}{4}-\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}})}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the denominator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the denominator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1/4)}\frac{4x-1}{2x-\sqrt{x}} & ={lim}_{x\to (1/4)}\frac{(4x-1)(2x+\sqrt{x})}{(2x-\sqrt{x})(2x+\sqrt{x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (1/4)}\frac{(4x-1)(2x+\sqrt{x})}{(2x)^{2}-(\sqrt{x})^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (1/4)}\frac{(4x-1)(2x+\sqrt{x})}{4{x}^{2}-x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (1/4)}\frac{(4x-1)(2x+\sqrt{x})}{x(4x-1)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (1/4)}\frac{\cancel{(4x-1)}(2x+\sqrt{x})}{x\cancel{(4x-1)}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (1/4)}\frac{2x+\sqrt{x}}{x} \\  & =\frac{(2\cdot \frac{1}{4}+\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}})}{(\frac{1}{4})} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Limit of a Rational Function with a Radical in the Denominator
questions.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit by simply evaluating the function at $x=3$, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{x-3}{3x-\sqrt{27x}} & =\frac{3-3}{3(3)-\sqrt{27(3)}}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the denominator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the denominator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{x-3}{3x-\sqrt{27x}} & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{(x-3)(3x+\sqrt{27x})}{(3x-\sqrt{27x})(3x+\sqrt{27x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{(x-3)(3x+\sqrt{27x})}{(3x)^{2}-(\sqrt{27x})^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{(x-3)(3x+\sqrt{27x})}{9{x}^{2}-27x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{(x-3)(3x+\sqrt{27x})}{9x(x-3)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{\cancel{(x-3)}(3x+\sqrt{27x})}{9x\cancel{(x-3)}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{3x+\sqrt{27x}}{9x} \\  & =\frac{3(3)+\sqrt{27(3)}}{9(3)} \\  & =\frac{9+9}{27} \\  & =\frac{18}{27} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
